exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV patient presents with fever and weight loss – what is the first investigation? — Blood cultures and TB screening; start empirical antibiotics if sepsis suspected.

A patient with chronic arthritis improves on anti‑TNF therapy but develops new pulmonary infiltrates – what is the likely complication? — Reactivation of latent TB; obtain sputum culture and start anti‑TB treatment.
During a septic shock episode, why is hydrocortisone added to fluids and vasopressors? — To blunt the cytokine storm and improve vascular tone.
A child with sickle cell crisis has persistent fever – how do you differentiate infection from vaso‑occlusive pain? — Look for leukocytosis, CRP elevation, and perform a blood culture.

In a low‑resource setting, a patient with high fever and hypotension has no available cultures – what empirical regimen covers the most likely TNF‑driven pathogens? — Broad‑spectrum beta‑lactam plus a macrolide or fluoroquinolone.
A patient on anti‑TNF therapy develops a new rash and arthralgia – what is the differential? — Drug reaction, infection (TB, viral), or disease flare.
When is anti‑TNF therapy contraindicated in a patient with chronic disease? — Active infection, uncontrolled TB, or hepatitis B/C.
ai.title: Tumor Necrosis Factor
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: TNF‑α is a cytokine that drives inflammation and tissue damage in many infections and autoimmune diseases. In low‑resource settings it is a key mediator of sepsis, TB, malaria and HIV‑related complications.

b: Elevated in sepsis, TB, malaria, HIV
sections.p: TNF‑α is a soluble protein produced mainly by macrophages and T cells. It is measured by ELISA or rapid point‑of‑care tests in research settings; clinically we infer its activity from clinical syndromes and response to anti‑TNF therapy.

t.b: Inflammatory marker – high CRP suggests active TNF‑driven inflammation
Elevated ESR supports chronic inflammatory state
Mild transaminitis may reflect cytokine‑mediated hepatocellular injury

b: WHO TB severity: high bacterial load, cavitation, weight loss
sections.p: TNF‑mediated disease severity is graded by clinical presentation and organ dysfunction. In sepsis, the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is used; in TB, the WHO TB severity scale guides treatment intensity.

b: Infections: TB, malaria, HIV, bacterial sepsis
Chronic diseases: rheumatic heart disease, schistosomiasis, sickle cell crisis
Herbal remedies: some contain endotoxins that stimulate TNF
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, TNF overproduction is triggered by infections and chronic inflammatory conditions.
TNF excess manifests as fever, malaise, weight loss, and organ dysfunction. In sepsis, it causes hypotension and multi‑organ failure; in TB it contributes to cachexia and pulmonary cavitation.
Laboratory and imaging confirm underlying cause and assess organ involvement. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and basic labs guide management.

t.b: Detects anemia, leukocytosis or leukopenia – leukocytosis suggests infection
Identify bacterial sepsis – absence of culture in low‑resource settings requires empirical therapy
Detects malaria parasites or schistosoma eggs

b: Septic shock: hypotension <90 mmHg, cold clammy skin
sections.p: Uncontrolled TNF can lead to septic shock, multi‑organ failure, and death. In TB, excessive TNF causes extensive lung destruction.
Treat the underlying cause first. Supportive care includes fluids, vasopressors and organ support. Anti‑TNF agents are reserved for chronic inflammatory diseases after infection screening.

t.b: Adjunct in septic shock – reduces inflammation
Used only after TB and HIV screening is negative

sections.p: Monitor clinical response, repeat CRP/ESR, and watch for drug toxicity. Prevention focuses on infection control, vaccination, and early treatment of chronic infections.

b: Severe malaria – look for parasites on smear
sections.p: Sepsis can mimic severe malaria; TB can resemble chronic pneumonia. Distinguish by specific tests and clinical context.
Low‑grade fever may be normal in HIV patients; CRP can be normal in early sepsis. Clinical vigilance is essential.

whenToSeekHelp: Septic shock (hypotension <90 mmHg), sudden respiratory failure, altered consciousness
